actionDeleteRecycle: Delete to Recycle Bin (file manager + Explorer takeover)
actionClipboardCapture: Open clipboard panel from any program
actionToggleWindow: Show the main window from any program; press again to hide it to the tray
fixedPalette: Command palette (search / jump to any panel)
fixedSelectAll: Select all in lists (clipboard / file manager)
files1: Pick files or whole folders to encrypt, or just drag them into the window - routed automatically by type: regular files get encrypted, .ivault files get decrypted.
files2: A folder is packed and encrypted into a single .ivault container; before decrypting a folder you first see the list of files inside and confirm.
files3: Batch jobs run 4-way concurrent with per-item progress; the rest of the app stays fully responsive while encrypting/decrypting.
files4: Decryption never overwrites existing files: if the target exists it refuses, and your original stays untouched.
fm1: Browse drives and copy/cut/paste/delete with the high-speed engine - faster than Explorer for big files and huge piles of small files.
fm2: Delete goes to the Recycle Bin by default; permanent delete is unrecoverable and shows a red confirmation first.
fm3: With "System-level file shortcuts" enabled, paste/delete inside real Explorer also use the high-speed engine (supports launch at startup; your customized keys apply there too).
fm4: Batch rename (numbering or find & replace mode) and right-click "Encrypt to Vault" / "Decrypt here" are built in.
clip1: Automatically records text and images you copy; click an entry to copy or paste it again.
clip2: Pin, hide (viewing requires re-verification), favorite snippets, and one-click conversions for code/URLs (JSON formatting, Base64, case, URL encode/decode).
clip3: Open the clipboard panel from any program with the global shortcut (default Ctrl+Shift+V, customizable).
clip4: The recycle bin supports multi-select / select-all bulk restore or permanent delete.
notes1: Import txt/md files or whole folders; imports are auto-classified by keywords, and subfolder names become category paths.
notes2: Categories support multi-level trees with "/" separators; edit each category's auto-classify keywords in category management - newly added categories join auto-classification too.
notes3: Large files open instantly: notes of hundreds of MB open on click with continuous scrolling and lag-free typing.
notes4: Markdown offers source/preview/split views; export to txt/docx/pdf; tags, full-text search, and auto-scroll live in the toolbar.
notes5: Create a note from any program with the global quick-note key (default Ctrl+Shift+N, customizable); edits auto-save with crash recovery.
pw1: Encrypted storage for sites/accounts/passwords, with one-click import from browser-exported CSV.
pw2: Built-in authenticator (TOTP codes) can replace a phone authenticator app.
pw3: Sort by recent use / alphabetical / site, plus search.
ai1: Translate, summarize, and polish clipboard or note content (configure the API in Settings first).
ai2: Chat history is stored in the local encrypted database - no third-party storage.
net1: Single- and multi-connection modes, showing download/upload/latency/jitter/loaded-latency plus a gaming rating.
net2: History supports filtering, trends, and CSV export.
set1: Change your password and rebind Windows Hello unlock, the authenticator or your recovery email; each module can individually require verification on entry.
set2: The "Keyboard shortcuts" section customizes 7 shortcuts: click a combo button and press the new combination - changes apply instantly and sync to the system-level engine.
set3: Launch at startup, txt/md file association, clipboard blacklist, and note storage mode all live in Settings.
set4: Switch dark/light mode under the View → Appearance menu; change the UI language with the switcher at the top of the sidebar.
shortcutsPanes: Jump to a panel (numbers match the sidebar)
fixedReload: Reload the interface (try this first if it freezes)
fixedCloseWindow: Close the window (goes to the tray, does not quit)
fixedQuit: Quit the app (closing the window only hides it)
sectionMenus: The menu bar: where things live
menu1: File — new note, open the file vault, open the file manager, Recent exports (one click reveals the file in Explorer), open settings, the system-wide file shortcuts toggle, hide to tray, quit.
menu2: Edit — undo/redo, cut/copy/paste, Paste as plain text (drops the styling that comes with anything copied from a web page), select all, delete to recycle bin / delete permanently (only clickable in the file manager panel), command palette.
menu3: View — jump to any of the eight panels, Appearance (follow system / light / dark), zoom, reload, full screen, settings, diagnostics.
menu4: Window — minimise, hide to tray, always on top, centre the window, reset to default size, close. If the window ends up off-screen (common after unplugging an external monitor) use “Centre the window” — the mouse cannot reach it at that point.
menu5: Help — this guide, check for updates, copy diagnostics (for when you ask someone for help; it contains none of your data), project home, report an issue, about.
cd1: 1. Scan a QR code (fastest): tap “Generate pairing code” here and “Scan” on the phone. Both sides then show six digits and six emoji — check they match exactly before tapping “They match”. Do not skip this: device names can be faked, and the safety code is the only thing that proves you are talking to the right device.
cd2: 2. Copy the pairing code: for devices without a camera. Send the CB1:… string across and let the other side paste it. A pairing code works once and expires in 60 seconds, so an old screenshot is harmless.
cd3: 3. Nearby devices: on the same Wi-Fi, just tap Pair in the list — no scanning, no copying.
cd4: 4. Enter an address: the fallback when nothing else works, and the most reliable one. The top of that tab shows this computer’s address (something like 192.168.1.7:52140) to read out; the bottom is where you type theirs. Any two devices that can reach each other by IP can pair — they do not have to be on the same subnet, and it works where multicast is blocked.
cd5: When the list is empty, use “Scan the network” rather than pressing “Refresh” again. Refresh only re-reads what has already been heard, and many routers drop the multicast packets automatic discovery relies on — in those networks refreshing a hundred times still shows nothing. Scanning asks every address directly and sidesteps the problem.
cd6: A yellow banner at the top of the page means Windows Firewall is blocking device discovery — tap “Allow it” (one system permission prompt; only home and private networks are opened). If it still will not connect, run the connection check: it goes through each step and tells you which one is failing.
cd7: Pick who gets it before you send. The toggle above the buttons is either “One device” (choose it from the dropdown) or “Several devices” (tick them in the list below). Files never go anywhere you did not pick — the Send button stays disabled until a target is chosen. The clipboard is different on purpose: it always syncs to every paired device, because a shared clipboard that only reaches one of them is not a shared clipboard.
cd8: Clear out the activity list. Tick individual rows and press Delete, or use “Clear all”. Failed rows are worth removing once you have dealt with them — they sit at the top of the list and there is nothing left to learn from them.
sectionAndroid: Android phone / tablet: step by step
and1: Step 1: open the app and allow notifications — transfer progress and pairing requests arrive through them. The home screen shows this device’s name and fingerprint.
and2: Step 2: pair with the computer. On the computer open Cross-device and tap “Generate pairing code”; on the phone tap “Scan”, allow the camera when asked, and line up the QR code.
and3: Step 3: both sides show six digits and six emoji. Check they match exactly, then tap “They match” on both. If they differ, the connection is being intercepted — tap “They differ” and it is voided immediately.
and4: Choose “long-term” when pairing your own phone (reconnects automatically, clipboard shared) or “temporary” for someone else’s device (expires, nothing written to disk).
and5: Day to day: copy anything and tap “Send clipboard”. For files use “Send files”, or the system Share menu from any app — the first time you may have to swipe right or tap “More” before Tessera appears.
and6: When it will not connect, in this order: 1. tap “Scan the network” (not “Refresh”) 2. run the connection check and see which step it points at 3. look for the firewall banner at the top of the page on the computer 4. fall back to “Enter an address”.
and7: Worth doing once on phones with aggressive power management: add Tessera to the battery-optimisation allowlist, permit background activity, and lock its card in the recents list. Otherwise the system kills the sync service once the screen goes off, which looks like “it disconnects after a while”.
and8: Sharing from another app now asks where to send. Long-press a photo or file → Share → Tessera. If more than one device is online you get a checklist (plus a “Send to all” button); with only one device online it just sends. You always get a confirmation, and if nothing is paired yet it says so instead of failing silently. Shared text goes to the clipboard of every paired device.
files5: Pick the algorithm right in the Encrypt card (AES-256-GCM / AES-128-GCM / ChaCha20-Poly1305). Decryption has no such choice - the algorithm is recorded inside the file and detected automatically.
clip5: The three counters at the top (total / pinned / hidden) are clickable filters. Clicking Hidden asks you to unlock first.
clip6: Maths and physics formulas are detected automatically (LaTeX fragments, symbols like ∫∑√ΔΩ) and filed under a Formula category. Content copied from Word's equation editor still pastes back into Office with its formatting.
clip7: Export scope: everything / pinned only / hidden only / selected only (multi-select and select-all both work). Import accepts several files at once and securely deletes each source file afterwards by default - export files are plaintext, so a leftover copy is an unprotected one.
notes6: Categories sort by name, note count or last used - or switch to Custom order and arrange them yourself. Switching to an automatic mode never discards your custom order.
pw4: The three counters (total / weak / reused) are clickable filters - click one and the list shows exactly those entries.
ai3: Pick the model from the dropdown in the AI assistant's title bar, or hit “Fetch list” in Settings to pull what the server offers. The choice applies to every AI feature in the app.
net3: The test discards TCP slow start before it starts counting and uses several parallel streams - that is what brings it in line with speedtest.net. The line under the result says which node it hit, how many streams, and how many seconds were counted.
set5: During first-time setup both the authenticator and Windows Hello can be skipped. Password and recovery key are always created, so skipping can never lock you out; you can add them later in Settings. Which method Windows Hello actually uses - fingerprint, face or PIN - is decided by Windows from what you enrolled in the system: the app cannot ask for a particular one, and it is never told which one you used. That is why a prompt labelled Hello sometimes asks for your PIN - nothing is misconfigured.
set6: The installer asks separately where the program goes and where your data goes - the program folder always lands inside a Tessera folder. Uninstalling asks once whether to delete your data too; the default is to keep it.
rc1: Keeps every site's two-factor backup codes in one place, encrypted with the same whole-database encryption as the password vault.
rc2: Import and export as TXT / CSV / JSON with multi-select and select-all; on import you choose whether to delete the source file (deleted by default, so plaintext codes do not stay on disk).
rc3: Grouped by provider automatically. Revealing plaintext can require re-verifying your identity first (toggle in Settings -> Content & features).
rc4: Recovery codes are an account's last line of defence - export a copy to offline media as well.
clean1: Five tabs: checkup, disk space, startup & menus, installed software, toolbox. Open it from the sidebar or press Ctrl + 9.
clean2: The checkup scans junk, browser caches, privacy traces, disk slimming, startup entries, the registry, plugins, ad-popup sources, memory and your own rules in parallel, filling the screen as each finishes rather than after all of them do.
clean3: Every entry carries one of five importance levels (system-critical / driver / common / optional / junk). System-critical entries can never be ticked; hover the badge to see why an entry got its level.
clean4: Junk is filtered by how long a file has gone untouched. Logs and caches are written to constantly, so the default 1-day threshold hides a large share of them - the list states how much was left out, and lowering the threshold under Scan depth includes it.
clean5: Browser caches are listed per profile, so you can clear one account without touching another. Caches are kept separate from cookies and history: clearing a cache never signs you out.
clean6: Duplicate-file and large-file analysis take minutes and each has a time budget. On timeout the panel says so and hands back what it did find - it never pretends the scan completed.
clean7: Every cleanup is recorded and can be undone. Deletions go to the Recycle Bin by default; permanent deletion asks separately.
sectionSecurityCheck: Security check-up, smart search, and hand-off
sec1: Sidebar → Other → Security check-up: encryption strength, backups, cross-device route and dependency vulnerabilities on one screen, with a 0-100 score.
sec2: Every item shows points earned out of points available, and they add up to the total — no hidden weighting, so you can check it yourself.
sec3: “Worth doing” comes first, and each row says what to do next. Hit “Run again” after a fix.
sec4: Items marked “not measured” are excluded from the score: not turning a feature on should not cost you points.
sec5: Ctrl+K global search understands pinyin initials (jdcwfp finds 季度财务复盘) and one-letter typos (passwrod → password).
sec6: Those guessed results are tagged “Fuzzy” on the right so you can tell them from literal matches.
sec7: With a note open on your PC, your phone shows a “still open on…” strip at the top. It only tells you — it never jumps anywhere. Tap the right side to dismiss it.
sec8: That strip disappears on its own after 90 seconds without an update, so shutting the PC down clears it too.
privacy1: Vault files, notes and passwords are encrypted and stay on this machine. They are never uploaded.
privacy2: The AI assistant sends the messages you type to DeepSeek’s cloud service. Do not enter passwords, one-time codes or ID numbers.
privacy3: With desktop control on, the AI reads on-screen interface text and sends it to the model. Do not let it handle passwords, one-time codes, payments or deletions.
